title: Frisians
capsule: The Frisians (Friezen) were a Germanic coastal people who occupied the marshlands and barrier islands of the southern North Sea from the Rhine delta to the Weser estuary, their loose political identity defined largely by resistance to Carolingian expansion and Frankish missionary activity. After the death of their last great independent king, Radbod, in 719, the Frisian lands were absorbed piecemeal from west to east; the conquest culminated with the subjugation of eastern Frisia by 785, in the wider context of Charlemagne's Saxon Wars. The atlas window of 793-800 thus falls in the immediate aftermath of incorporation, when Frisia was being integrated into the Frankish realm; the Lex Frisionum, codified under Frankish auspices around 785-802, preserved a distinctive Frisian customary law within the empire.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Frisian settlement zones are archaeologically and textually attested along the North Sea coast, but the extent of any unified Frisian political territory in this narrow window is poorly defined and largely conventional.
